trials.name: Pilot Phase 2 Trial of GM-CSF (Leukine) in Alzheimer's Disease
trials.population: Adults 55-85 years old with mild-to-moderate Alzheimer's disease (MMSE 10-26) and elevated cortical amyloid
trials.results_summary: Sargramostim was generally safe. While MMSE scores showed a 1.45 unit improvement from a significantly lower baseline, ADAS-Cog13 scores worsened compared to placebo at follow-up.

trials.name: Phase II Trial to Evaluate Safety and Efficacy of GM-CSF/Sargramostim in Alzheimer's Disease
trials.population: Adults 60-85 years old with probable mild or moderate Alzheimer's disease and positive amyloid biomarkers
trials.primary_endpoint: Safety as measured by number of Adverse Events (AEs) by body system

trials.name: Safety Study of Sargramostim in Treating Patients With Mild Cognitive Impairment Due to Alzheimer's Disease
trials.population: Adults 40-80 years old with mild cognitive impairment (MCI) due to Alzheimer's disease
trials.primary_endpoint: Change from baseline in standardized uptake value ratio as measured by PET using florbetapir F18 (Amyvid)

related_evidence.description: Phase II trial reporting safety, immune activation, and mixed cognitive outcomes for sargramostim in Alzheimer's disease.
ClinicalTrials.gov results posting for NCT01409915 showing baseline imbalances and mixed cognitive outcomes.

evidence_assessment: The clinical evidence for sargramostim (GM-CSF) in Alzheimer's disease relies almost entirely on a single, short-duration (3-week treatment), underpowered (N=40 analyzed) Phase 2 trial (NCT01409915). While the trial met its primary safety endpoint and showed exploratory improvements in MMSE and some plasma biomarkers, these findings are severely confounded by a significant baseline cognitive imbalance between the treatment and placebo groups. Furthermore, the standard cognitive endpoint ADAS-Cog13 showed no benefit and actually worsened at follow-up. An earlier Sanofi-sponsored Phase 2 trial (NCT02667496) was withdrawn due to slow recruitment, leaving an ongoing Phase 2 trial (NCT04902703) as the only active attempt to replicate these highly preliminary and tenuous findings. Overall, current evidence is weak and insufficient to demonstrate clinical cognitive efficacy.
discrepancies: The document claims 'no drug-related serious adverse events', but the registry lists 1 serious adverse event (Myocardial Infarction) in the sargramostim group, which was presumably deemed unrelated by investigators.

The registry confirms the document's red flag of severe baseline imbalance in cognitive scores (MMSE: placebo 20.75 vs sargramostim 17.10; ADAS-Cog13: placebo 36.20 vs sargramostim 43.20), casting doubt on the reliability of the cognitive benefit claims.

While the document highlights MMSE improvement, the registry results show that on the ADAS-Cog13 scale, the sargramostim group worsened at the 45-day follow-up (score increased from 43.20 to 47.67) compared to placebo (36.20 to 36.33).
